cells.tense: You're here in it now, and the sorting isn't costing you anything — you can say what's true in the room without needing to win it.
cells.ask: The next time something good is happening between you and someone, say out loud what you notice is working — before you leave the table.
cells.core:
You notice what's real in a conversation and you say it without having to make it land. If a friend is half-telling you something, you can feel the true shape of it and you can leave it be until they get there. That's rare and it doesn't feel like effort.

What you're free to feed next is the plain version. There's a pull toward keeping your read private, holding every reading so nothing gets decided. The structure underneath that serves what it organizes — if you say what you see, the funny-bitter-sad shape of it is what the other person can align to, and you're the one who named it.
cells.sheetLine: You can tell what's real in the room and say it without pushing.
cells.verb: telling what is real from what is close to it, and holding what you find
cells.place: the part of life where you're in it with someone and trying to stay aligned

cells.tense: You're already reading how this lands before you say anything, rehearsing the conversation that hasn't happened — and you're living there instead of here.
cells.ask: Pick one conversation you've been pre-writing in your head. Say one honest sentence in it this week and stop there — let the rest come from them.
cells.core:
On an ordinary day this works when you can talk with someone and not need to know how it goes — you say the one true thing you have, then you're quiet, and the outcome stays partly theirs. Talking with someone and leaving the next move open is the whole skill, and you have it.

Right now you're ahead of the moment, working out which version of the truth they'll accept and shaping your words for that one. Your head is in a conversation that hasn't started, and the version of you that's actually present is somewhere behind it. You get to set one direction for the conversation instead of ten — say the thing once, aim it at the person, and see what comes back.
cells.sheetLine: You're answering a conversation that hasn't happened yet.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a moment that already happened — you saw something about someone and you didn't say it, and you've been outside the conversation since.
cells.ask: Think of one person you've been holding back from. Tell them one true thing you see about what they're going through — in their own kitchen terms, not a report.
cells.core:
This runs well when you're in a room with someone and you just say what you notice about them — that they look worn down, that something's landed, that you're glad they came — and you stay there while they take it or don't.

What's missing is being in the room at all. You watch from outside and call it not interfering, and meanwhile the connection you'd want doesn't get made. You don't have to force feeling — just give one honest observation to one person and let the two of you be in it together for a minute. What you see lands differently when it's spoken to a face.

cells.tense: You're steering things with people right now — how you come across, what you let them think — and you talk about it like it's just how people get along.
cells.ask: Pick one thing this week where you quietly decided what's fair and tell the other person your reasoning out loud — one sentence, once, and let them answer.
cells.core:
In a good week, you can be with someone and you know who's owed what, and you act on it plainly. You give back the favor, you tell the truth about a small thing, you say the agreement out loud — and people trust you about the details because you're fair about them.

What's happening instead is that the deciding is already done and no one gets to see it. The call about who deserves what has been made privately and quietly, and you're sitting in that same room like the fairness was obvious. The older, simpler form of this is just saying what you decide is right. That doesn't mean defending it or making them agree — one sentence of reasoning, out loud, where they can hear it, is enough.

A reader could reasonably say 'my problem isn't too many truths, it's not knowing my own mind' — so the core stays on the sorting that happens between people, which is what this seat can support.
